articles.title: No November 17 blackout, this is only a test: FEMA to send emergency alert tones on radio, TV at 2.20 PM ET as a routine check
articles.summary: The US is preparing for a nationwide emergency alert test on Tuesday, November 17, but the scheduled exercise has triggered a wave of online speculation
articles.body: The US is preparing for a nationwide emergency alert test on Tuesday, November 17, but the scheduled exercise has triggered a wave of online speculation about a possible blackout, internet shutdown and disruption of essential services. The rumours have also revived claims that the animated television series The Simpsons predicted a major blackout on the same date.The Federal Emergency Management Agency, in coordination with the Federal Communications Commission, will conduct a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System at approximately 2:20 pm Eastern Time on November 17. Officials reiterated that this is a routine test of the country's emergency communication infrastructure and is not connected to any planned power outage or national emergency.FEMA also took to social media to address the speculation surrounding the test. “We’ve heard a lot of rumors about tomorrow’s EAS test,” the agency said in a post on Monday, adding that there would be “no blackouts, no secret emergencies”.What will happen during the November 17 emergency alert test?The test will be broadcast through television and radio networks across the country. It is expected to last approximately one minute, interrupting regular programming with an alert tone and a message explaining that it is only a nationwide test.The message will identify FEMA as the issuing agency and explicitly state that no action is required from the public.Importantly, Tuesday's exercise will not involve wireless emergency alerts on mobile phones. Unlike the October 2023 nationwide test, which included alerts sent directly to cellphones, the November 17 exercise is limited to the Emergency Alert System.The EAS operates through participating radio and television broadcasters, cable and satellite television providers and other media services. It is designed to distribute important information to the public during emergencies, including natural disasters and threats to public safety.The test is required under federal law, which mandates nationwide testing of the emergency alert infrastructure at least once every three years. The previous nationwide test took place in October 2023.If an actual emergency or significant weather event requires postponement, FEMA and the FCC have December 3, 2026, as the backup date.Why are rumours of a November 17 blackout spreading?Social media posts have been circulating claims that November 17 will mark the beginning of a 90-day nationwide blackout in the US. Some versions of the rumour go further, alleging that internet services, banking systems and digital infrastructure will be shut down for three months.The claims gained traction amid recent disruptions to major technology services, including Microsoft's outage and the FAA's nationwide flight ground stop, which raised concerns about the reliability of critical infrastructure.Some viral posts have also used an edited video of President Donald Trump to suggest that he announced an impending 90-day blackout. However, the footage was manipulated and Trump did not make such an announcement during the November 9 White House briefing.The rumours have also been linked to a Pentagon initiative announced in September called FORTRESS America, which aims to ensure that major military installations can maintain independent power and essential resources during potential disruptions. The initiative is about military preparedness, not an announcement of an impending nationwide blackout.There is no official warning or credible evidence that the US is preparing for a 90-day power outage, internet shutdown or banking disruption on November 17.Did ‘The Simpsons’ predict the November 17 blackout?The speculation has also drawn attention to a 2023 episode of The Simpsons, with social media users claiming that the long-running animated series predicted a major blackout on November 17, 2026.The viral theory centres on the Season 35 episode titled “It's a Blunderful Life”, which features a fictional power outage in Springfield. In the episode, an older Lisa recalls a blackout that left the town without electricity for six days. A reference to November 17 in the storyline has prompted viewers to connect the fictional event to Tuesday's date.The episode does not predict a worldwide or nationwide blackout on November 17, 2026. Nor does it establish any connection between the fictional power outage and the scheduled FEMA exercise.The episode originally aired on November 19, 2023. The date reference in its storyline is being taken out of context and linked to the 2026 calendar by social media users.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Impeach Hegseth? Not when Democrats don’t show up
articles.summary: Had the Democrats shown up and voted with their colleagues, they would have had the numbers to defeat the procedural move to table the measure.
articles.body:
Last week, in a bizarre twist of fate, it was the absence of 11 Democratic lawmakers that spared Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth a devastating rebuke and possible ouster after an election that expressed voter discontent about the Iran war.

The turn of events was surprising as Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), soon to be Speaker of the House of Representatives, had just told ABC that an impeachment of Hegseth was a “hard yes,” as a bipartisan coalition of congressmen tried to set the table for Hegseth’s ouster.

Had the Democrats shown up and voted with their colleagues, they would have had the numbers to defeat the procedural move to table the measure, forcing an early House vote on impeachment. No Defense secretary in history has been the subject of as much scorn as Hegseth. And there is much ado in the to do.

Writers across the political spectrum have scorned his conduct with a heavy bill of particulars. This ranges from waging unauthorized war against Iran and a lack of preparedness following Iranian attacks on U.S. supply hubs in the Persian Gulf to lethal U.S. military strikes on suspected drug-smuggling vessels in Latin America. Those extrajudicial killings, which lack valid legal justification, included secondary strikes to kill survivors clinging to wreckage after an initial attack.

There’s also the removal of top-ranking military officers and the blocking of senior promotions over perceived adherence to diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives. Finally, there’s retaliation against political critics such as Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) and a lack of transparency in withholding Pentagon press briefings for six months , evading public accountability for failures in the Iranian war effort.

Since it was unlikely that President Trump would fire Hegseth even under such a formidable barrage of pressure, the obvious remedy would be impeachment. Leading the charge was Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who authored the House resolution listing eight separate charges against Hegseth, largely mirroring the media criticism. Massie has long been a staunch critic of Hegseth.

The Republican-led House won, 211 to 204 , on a procedural motion to refer the impeachment back to the House Judiciary Committee, where it could remain indefinitely. The procedural move killed the impeachment drive for the duration of the current term, ending Jan. 3, 2027, when Democrats will take control of Congress.

The action indefinitely delayed the vote on whether to impeach Hegseth on those charges , including violating the Constitution to wage war in Iran and Yemen without congressional authorization, flouting laws to mitigate civilian casualties and abusing his power by retaliating against a senator for public statements.

Democratic politicians and progressive commentators have expressed outrage that poor attendance from Democrats affected the outcome of the vote.

Some pundits pointed the finger at Jeffries, accusing him of failing to exert sufficient pressure on party members to defeat the measure. Jeffries has said he will consult members about another possible bid to impeach Hegseth next year. “ We’ll have that conversation ,” Jeffries said, calling Hegseth “the most unqualified secretary of defense in American history.” He stopped, however, at calling for Hegseth’s impeachment.

If convicted after impeachment, Hegseth would be immediately removed from office. But, for conviction, the Constitution requires at least a two-thirds concurring vote in the Senate. That means Senate Democrats, even with their incoming majority in the chamber next year, would likely need about a dozen Republicans to join them to secure Hegseth’s removal.

Trump said the vote was an “ exoneration ” of Hegseth. Hardly. The outcome gave him an unexpected reprieve, but only for a while. Democrats could still move to impeach him next year when they assume power.

Hegseth’s standing in the administration was further thrown into question following sweeping Republican losses in the midterm elections. It had not been clear whether Republican lawmakers, including several who were unexpectedly defeated or won reelection far more narrowly than they anticipated, would rally to support him. It was no accident that seven Republicans didn’t show up for the vote either. In the end, though, more Democrats than Republicans missed the vote.

The vote came hours after Hegseth defiantly defended himself at a Pentagon news briefing, equating the criticisms of him to critiques of American troops. “I stand behind every one of these operations,” he said of the military actions cited in the articles as unlawful conduct. “I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow.”

Some Republicans who had expressed dissatisfaction with Hegseth’s performance ultimately concluded that impeachment was not the appropriate remedy, noting that Hegseth served at the pleasure of the president, and that any decision to fire him rested with Trump.

Others had privately raised concerns that the articles of impeachment, which include wide-ranging allegations of misconduct when overseeing military operations, only reflected policy disputes within the Pentagon.

Vice President Vance made a spirited defense of Hegseth, saying that the impeachment effort was nothing more than political theater.

“Has Pete Hegseth committed impeachable crimes?” asked Vance . “The question is absurd and the answer is: obviously not.”

James D. Zirin is a former federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York and a published legal analyst.

articles.title: UK sanctions eight Israeli construction firms over West Bank settlements
articles.summary: Settler group also sanctioned for blocking Gaza aid as foreign secretary calls for ‘protecting the two-state solution’.
articles.body:
The government of the United Kingdom has imposed sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and a settler group blocking aid to Gaza.

The companies affected in Tuesday’s asset freezes include Har Hevron Development Company Ltd, Hemdat Shomron Ltd and SAG (Velvel) Construction and Development Ltd, which construct and develop homes in West Bank settlements, which are illegal under international law.

The measures were announced shortly before the final deadlines for the tenders for E1, a settlement project that would bisect the West Bank and cut it off from occupied East Jerusalem, fragmenting the land Palestinians hope will form the heart of an independent state.

“Protecting the two-state solution is the North Star of this Government’s approach,” British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said in a statement. “That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution.”

The government also imposed sanctions on Tzav 9, a group it said had regularly blocked humanitarian aid trucks from delivering food, water and fuel to the Gaza Strip.

Reporting from London, Al Jazeera’s Jonah Hull said the sanctions on Tzav 9 come after the UK’s Foreign and Commonwealth Office has noted that thousands of families in Gaza are in dire need of aid after “catastrophic” floods .

Britain’s relationship with Israel has deteriorated significantly over the past three years because of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza as well as the Israeli government’s plans to expand settlements in the West Bank.

Israel in September threatened to close the British consulate building in East Jerusalem in response to London’s decision to impose trade sanctions on Israeli settlements.

British and Israeli diplomats last month reached a last-minute agreement to avoid the closure.

Meanwhile on Tuesday, Israeli forces carried out a series of raids and arrests in the West Bank, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.

A Palestinian woman was killed in an attack on Monday night by Israeli settlers firing live ammunition at Palestinians in the area of the village of Ein ad-Duyuk at-Tahta in Jericho governorate, according to medical sources.

The Jericho Governmental Hospital reported that 10 Palestinians were injured by the settlers’ gunfire, including an elderly man.

Israeli soldiers also raided the Jalazone refugee camp and arrested two people in addition to arresting another person from el-Bireh after searching a home.

Troops also stormed Nablus, Tubas and the villages of Khallet al-Louza and Beit Falouh in Bethlehem governorate, raiding homes and shops and firing tear gas.

articles.summary: President Trump said Tuesday that Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on U.S. exports and remove substantial nontariff barriers on a number of products as part of a trade deal the two countries will be finalizing. Trump and Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul signed a joint statement saying they have “reached substantial conclusion” in their trade…
articles.body:
President Trump said Tuesday that Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on U.S. exports and remove substantial nontariff barriers on a number of products as part of a trade deal the two countries will be finalizing.

Trump and Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul signed a joint statement saying they have “reached substantial conclusion” in their trade negotiations.

The two leaders signed the agreement in Manila, Philippines, ahead of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit.

“Today’s deal lays the foundation for a much stronger trading relationship that will bring the United States and Thailand closer than ever before,” Trump said.

“Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on U.S. exports, which is something we’ve been after for a long time,” he continued, “and remove substantial nontariff barriers on American vehicles, medical devices, pharmaceuticals, ethanol and poultry.”

He also said Thailand will be buying roughly $2.6 billion in additional U.S. agricultural products, and the deal will be finalized in the coming weeks.

“We’ve been working on this deal for a long time,” he said.

The U.S. is Thailand’s largest export market.

This follows a framework for a trade agreement reached last October, when Thailand agreed to eliminate tariffs on 99 percent of goods from the U.S.

Anutin said he was “pleased” the conclusion was reached.

“I’m confident that the agreement will be ready for us to sign real soon,” he said. “Thailand attaches great importance to its long-standing relationship with the United States.”

articles.title: These are the ‘world’s coolest’ streets for 2026, according to Time Out
articles.summary: Time Out’s “coolest streets” round-up celebrates the world’s best promenades and pathways. Here’s which street came out on top for this year.
articles.body: There’s no better way to get a sense of a new city than strolling down one of its streets — checking out street art, window shopping at boutique stores and coffee-shop-hopping can be some of the best parts of a vacation. So which ones should be on your travel itinerary? International listing guide Time Out has some ideas on its newly released annual “coolest streets” list. “In our eyes, a cool street is somewhere locals actually want to spend their time,” Time Out editor Grace Beard tells CNN Travel. “It’s unique to its city, home to indie businesses, events or festivals you wouldn’t find elsewhere.” Topping this year’s list is Song Wat Road, Bangkok — a creative hub near the city’s Chao Phraya River. CNN Travel’s Karla Cripps, who has lived in Thailand for over 20 years, says she’s not shocked Song Wat came in at number one. “Soi Songwat has been becoming more popular for a few years now, with many creative entrepreneurs renovating the area’s old shophouses and warehouses to give them a second life, alongside the traditional businesses that continue to operate in the area,” says Cripps. “You can visit any time of day, but I really love going there at sunset, when the temperature starts to cool off, and have a drink next to the Chao Phraya River then wander around exploring the area’s shops, cafes, bars, street art and restaurants.” ‘Brilliant cross-section’ of city life Time Out leans on its global network of editors and writers to compile its annual list of 28 must-visit thoroughfares. The team makes nominations from cities around the world, which are then assessed by a panel of editors who consider food and drink options, shopping, nightlife, street life, community and local businesses. At number two on this year’s list is Golborne Road, a West London spot that Time Out’s Beard calls “a brilliant cross-section” of the city. Time Out highlights the street’s array of Portuguese, Moroccan and Middle Eastern eateries that give Golborne Road the nickname “Little Morocco.” And while Beard says the street is “unpretentious,” it’s also a bit of a celeb haunt — famous folk flock to renowned vintage store Relik and popular party pub The Fat Badger. “I love Golborne Road because of its multicultural feel, which I think is often overlooked when people talk about Notting Hill,” George Williams, head chef of the Fat Badger, tells CNN Travel. “There are brilliant Portuguese cafés, Moroccan restaurants and traditional food shops, reflecting the mix of different communities that make the area what it is.” Adam Zomlot, owner of Palestinian-Mediterranean café Maramia, namechecked by Time Out in its list, says Golborne Road is “a street with its own soul, and that’s something you can’t create overnight.” Zomlot adds that Golborne Road has “never needed to follow trends to be cool. It’s always had its own identity, its own character and its own magic. We’re just happy that the rest of the world is discovering what we’ve loved about it for years.” At number three on Time Out’s street round-up is Fernández de Enciso in Villa Devoto, an area of Buenos Aires also named one of Time Out’s coolest neighbourhoods in 2025. Time Out praises this street — and the area more broadly — as a foodie hotspot, and great place for locals and visitors alike to gather and enjoy. Vaasankatu in Helsinki, Finland comes in at four on Time Out’s list, a compact street that packs a punch restaurant-wise. Rounding out the top five is Neil Road, Singapore, which Time Out calls “one of Singapore’s most eclectic and progressive streets.” ‘Palpable buzz’ Coolness, of course, is subjective — something Beard acknowledges, but she says what unites all the streets on Time Out’s 2026 list is their “palpable buzz.” And while big hitting cities like London and New York feature on the list — New York City’s Atlantic Avenue is number 17 — Beard says Time Out made an effort for 2026 to “celebrate destinations beyond the usual tourist trail.” Beard points, for example, to the fact Japanese capital Tokyo is absent from the list, but streets in the Japanese cities of Kyoto and Fukuoka feature instead (Sanjo-dori in Kyoto is number 13, while Oyafuko Street in Fukuoka is number 25). The aim, says Beard, is “encouraging travelers to look further afield and discover the brilliant streets that give cities their character.” Even so, some of the world’s coolest streets can be both some of the most beloved and the busiest. CNN Travel’s Cripps, for example, points out that in the case of number one street Song Wat Road, “the secret is out and it can get very busy with locals and tourists.” Time Out’s Coolest Streets for 2026

articles.title: US loses measles elimination status after 26 years amid record case numbers
articles.summary: States have reported over 5,400 cases and 10 measles-related deaths for the first time since the early 1990s.
articles.body:
After more than two decades, the US has lost its measles-free status, following two years of record case numbers and deaths.

The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a specialised service of the United Nations, determined the US has had uninterrupted transmission of the same strain of measles for more than 12 months.

Dr Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO, announced that Mexico and Bolivia have also lost their measles elimination status, attributing the resurgence in the region to persistent "gaps in vaccination".

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said it was committed to "regaining measles elimination status" by expanding access to vaccines.

The US has seen 5,400 cases of measles this year alone, with 10 measles-related deaths, the most the country has seen since the 1990s.

The measles virus - with its signature blotchy red rash - used to infect millions of children a year before a vaccine was invented. The extremely contagious virus can be fatal, and some patients can experience long-term complications including encephalitis and immune amnesia, which resets the immune system, leaving it with only limited ability to respond to new infections.

The US recommends two measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) shots for children between ages one and six, which is 97% effective in protecting against the illness.

PAHO, a group within the World Health Organization, revoked the US's measles-elimination after determining that the virus had circulated nonstop for more than a year.

"These figures are a serious warning for our region," PAHO's director Barbosa said at a news conference on Tuesday. "Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination."

He added that Canada, which lost its status of having eliminated measles last year after seeing several large outbreaks, has made strides this year to interrupt transmission.

Daniel Salas, the executive manager of immunisations at PAHO, said that the US and others who lost elimination status would be required to submit corrective action plans outlining how they would attempt to improve vaccination rates.

US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr Kennedy has attempted to make a series of sweeping changes to US vaccine recommendations and policies. The vaccine sceptic has also frequently cast doubt on the safety of MMR shot, as vaccination rates have declined across the US in recent years.

Kennedy has argued that the rise in measles cases started before he took the helm at HHS and that neighbouring countries have also seen more infections.

Responding to Tuesday's announcement, the CDC said the agency and its partners were "committed to stopping measles outbreaks, protecting Americans, and regaining measles elimination status".

"Together, we will encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection," the agency said.

CDC Director Erica Schwartz said the measles elimination designation was not what protected Americans.

"Vaccination does," she said. "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities."

In a post on social media, Kennedy said: "I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles."

"We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust," he also said. "We will answer families' questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment."

The UK, Spain and Austria were among European nations that lost their measles-free status earlier this year, along with countries including Russia, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan.

Nuwan Gunawardhana, an assistant professor of medicine with Columbia University Irving Medical Center, said the US losing its elimination status was "a huge leap backwards".

The US was the first country to eliminate measles in the Americas thanks to vaccination campaigns, noted William Moss, a paediatric infectious disease specialist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.

Dr Gunawardhana said it took massive efforts from public health officials and clinicians to build trust with patients to increase uptake of the MMR vaccine, leading to decades in the US with few infections and deaths.

But that trust has been steadily eroding since the Covid-19 pandemic, when Dr Gunawardhana said patients were confronted with misinformation about the safety of vaccines and lost even more trust in public health systems.

The vaccination rate for MMR across the US has fallen to 92.4%, below the 95% level that provides herd immunity, which limits the spread of measles and protects those who cannot get vaccinated, including newborns.

An outbreak in Pennsylvania has infected over 1,400 people - likely a large underestimate - and killed seven people, according to state officials.

Kennedy, the health secretary, has sparred with Pennsylvania officials over how it is counting the measles deaths, with CDC declining for now to record some of the deaths in its database.

Last year, the health secretary fired all the members of a top vaccine advisory panel and replaced them with his own appointees, some of whom were vaccine critics.

The panel recommended a number of vaccine changes - including no longer requiring the Hepatitis B vaccine for all newborns - but those recommendations were blocked by a federal judge.

President Donald Trump this year also cast doubt on the safety of the MMR vaccine, issuing an executive order for the shot to be split into three separate immunisations for measles, mumps and rubella, a move public health experts say is costly and could sow confusion about an already safe vaccine.

Doctors and public health officials say the misinformation from Kennedy and Trump has played a major role in falling vaccination rates.

"It's confusing patients. It's confusing families," Dr Gunawardhana said. "We need a clear message from the top."

The federal government's vaccine manoeuvres have left public health officials and states to fill in the gaps, offering their own separate recommendations upholding decades-long practices.

articles.title: O’Reilly: ‘Trump may be wrong in the way he handles Xi and Putin’
articles.summary: Commentator Bill O’Reilly said Monday the way President Trump interacts with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin may not be successful. “Trump may be wrong in the way he handles Xi and Putin by trying to get them into a circle of agreement. That may not work, but that’s what he’s trying…
articles.body:
Commentator Bill O’Reilly said Monday the way President Trump interacts with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin may not be successful.

“Trump may be wrong in the way he handles Xi and Putin by trying to get them into a circle of agreement. That may not work, but that’s what he’s trying to do,” O’Reilly told NewsNation’s Leland Vittert on “On Balance.”

“You don’t go to China and insult Xi. That gets you nowhere. Xi’s not going to buckle to you. You go in and you try to convince them, all right, that a cyber war will wipe out everybody,” he added.

Trump has been notably friendly toward both Xi and Putin, who both lead governments that have had historically adversarial relationships with the U.S. Trump, Putin and Xi are set to meet Wednesday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China. Trump has said that global conflict is central to the upcoming meeting.

In September, Trump lavishly welcomed Xi for a two-day summit in Washington, D.C. He kicked off Xi’s visit with a rare tarmac greeting at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland that featured a red carpet and a canon salute.

The trilateral meeting also follows a recent scandal involving the founder of tech company Nvidia, Jensen Huang. Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang, who U.S. officials concluded passed information to Beijing. However, China has denied that she is a spy.

On Monday, Trump said that he wouldn’t mind seeing the Nvidia founder brought back as CEO after he resigned last week amid extramarital affairs with multiple women.

“I would not mind. I would not mind that,” Trump told reporters before heading to Asia.

“I think he learned a big lesson,” he continued. “I guess maybe one lesson more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that.”

articles.title: Election-winning student movement enters Serbia’s new parliament
articles.summary: Hundreds hail Student List lawmakers as the new parliament meets for the first time.
articles.body:
Following the October 25 vote that upended Serbia’s political landscape, the new parliament is meeting for the first time in Belgrade.

The vote redrew Serbia’s parliamentary map as a grassroots, student-led movement won the largest single share, removing President Aleksandar Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).

The Student List group was backed by 2.3 million citizens, altering the previous parliamentary arithmetic and balance of power. It holds a majority with 140 parliamentary seats in the 250-member parliament, compared with the Serbian Progressive Party’s 104.

Tuesday’s session is chaired by the oldest member of parliament until a new speaker is elected, assisted by the four youngest MPs from the largest electoral lists. Hundreds of supporters cheered the new lawmakers as they entered the National Assembly. The new speaker could be announced later on Tuesday.

The formal agenda follows a clear legal framework: verifying parliamentary mandates based on a report by the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK), taking the solemn oath of office, electing the speaker and deputy speakers, appointing the secretary-general, and forming parliamentary committees and permanent delegations to international bodies.

But beyond legal formalities, the political atmosphere is complex and large sections of the public have high expectations.

Political analyst Djordje Vukadinovic told Al Jazeera, “Everyone is eagerly awaiting it. I would avoid making any predictions, because with the current opposition structure, you never know what might happen or what stance they will take.”

He added, “What I do know is that this is only the beginning of establishing a new government, and I believe not everything will be wrapped up today.”

Ahead of the session, a group of students wrote to the new lawmakers, reminding them of their “serious” responsibilities.

“All of you are becoming members of parliament in the highest legislative body of the Republic of Serbia for the first time. And only that. Nothing more. The fact that the highest state offices have for decades been presented as ‘comfortable armchairs’ is a systemic flaw. The people elected you. We are the people. You are the people. Act accordingly,” warned the Student Plenum of the Higher School of Civil Engineering and Geodesy in Belgrade in an open letter.

Aleksandar Cupic, an incoming Student List MP and an assistant professor in engineering, said new lawmakers must demonstrate institutional maturity.

“We do not plan to speak about our candidate for five or 10 hours, because that is neither in the spirit of the values we will represent nor is it rational. We owe it to the citizens to proceed with electing the speaker of parliament,” Cupic told reporters ahead of the session.

He said political groups had been consulting one another in a more moderate atmosphere than reports have suggested.

But on Tuesday, tensions were seen outside parliament.

A woman threw yoghurt over Lidija Vukicevic, a well known actress who supports the SNS, outside parliament and the crowd booed Vucic as he walked in.

The swearing-in session marks the start of a critical political countdown – a 90-day constitutional deadline to elect a new government.

Should that expire without parliament voting in a new cabinet, Serbia’s constitution mandates the dissolution of the National Assembly and the calling of snap parliamentary elections.

The developments are being watched across the region, as well as in European and global political circles.

Observers say the new political leaders will have to govern the state and rebuild sustainable cooperation with neighbouring countries and the European Union – ties that have been strained in recent years.

Echoing that point, Student List representative Aleksandar Baucal told the international EU Enlargement Forum in Brussels that a peaceful transfer of power is only the start of a complex array of work.

“Changing power through non-violent and democratic means is only the first step,” Baucal said in Brussels. “Serbia now faces the task of rebuilding institutions that will prevent the personalisation of power and serve all citizens, regardless of who they voted for. I am convinced that from now on, the news coming out of Serbia will be largely positive.”

In a similar vein, the European Democratic Party (EDP) weighed in on the eve of the parliamentary session.

“Serbia must now heal the wounds of recent years through truth, justice and accountability … we sincerely hope a new chapter of freedom, democracy and reconciliation will begin,” the EDP said, adding that the session will test whether Serbia is ready for institutional reform.

articles.title: Luton-born Charles Bronson denied parole for ninth time
articles.summary: A Parole Board panel says his release will not be "safe for the protection of the public".
articles.body:
Charles Bronson, one of the UK's longest-serving inmates, has been refused release after his ninth parole hearing.

Bronson, 73, from Luton, has spent much of the last 50 years in prison following his conviction for armed robbery in 1974, including a period at HMP Woodhill in Milton Keynes.

The Parole Board panel found that Bronson, who now uses the name Charles Salvador, had committed "further incidents of violence against staff and other prisoners".

The panel was not satisfied that his release from HMP Wakefield would be "safe for the protection of the public", citing his "limited progress" in custody and the other evidence before it.

Oral evidence was heard from three members of staff responsible for the prisoner's management, none of whom - nor the authors of reports including a prison psychologist - supported his release.

Bronson, whose real name is Michael Peterson, was first convicted when he was 21, and jailed for seven years for robbery, aggravated burglary, assault with intent to rob and possession of a firearm.

His time in prison has included 11 hostage-taking incidents across nine sieges involving prison governors, doctors, prison staff and, on one occasion, his own solicitor.

Who is notorious prisoner Charles Bronson?

Bronson's eighth hearing was only the second parole hearing in the UK to be held in public.

He told the panel he dreamed of walking barefoot on grass and wanted his elderly mother to see him released before she died.

He said: "It's no secret I have had more porridge than Goldilocks and the Three Bears, and I'm sick of it. I've had enough of it. I want to go home."

Earlier this year, Bronson applied for his latest parole hearing to be held in public but the request was refused because there were insufficient resources to do so.

Parole board member Jeremy Roberts KC said he was prepared to accept that Bronson's reasons for seeking another public hearing were "entirely genuine even if (as is likely) there is an element of attention-seeking in his application".

The 73-year-old chose not to attend his latest parole hearing earlier this month, but told the panel through his lawyer that he accepted he would not be released or transferred to open conditions.

articles.title: Art of the immigration deal: Can Trump and Democrats find common ground?
articles.summary: Democrats might get the support they need to establish the following legalization programs individually or together in a single bill.
articles.body:
The Democrats will have a majority in the House and the Senate next year, but they may not be able to pass immigration reform legislation without Republican support. They won’t have the 60 votes needed to end a filibuster that is preventing the Senate from voting on Democratic legislation. And they aren’t likely to have enough votes to override a presidential veto , either.

But President Trump has said he would “love to do something on immigration ” with Democrats next year, suggesting a deal for “some immigrants who have been in the U.S. for 10 or 15 years and work in jobs such as landscaping or hotels.”

His support could sway enough Republican senators to make the passage of an immigration reform bill possible.

Moreover, “newly elected Democrats and strategists at the ‘What’s Next’ conference in Denver told Fox News Digital that their party should seek opportunities to work with Trump .” Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas) said at that conference that “the American people cannot wait two years for change. So we must work with President Trump.”

Democrats might get the support they need to establish the following legalization programs individually or together in a single bill.

During his first term in office, Trump offered a four-pillar legalization program for 1.8 million undocumented immigrants who were eligible for the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals or DACA program, which allows work authorization in the U.S. for undocumented immigrants who were brought to the U.S. when they were children.

The first pillar was to secure the border, which has been established already; the second, the legalization program; the third, eliminating the Diversity Lottery ; and the fourth, ending chain migration .

Trump’s legalization program did not get sufficient support, but it may be worth trying it again.

In my view, the main deal killer was requiring an end to chain migration. Instead, the administration could create a separate legalization program for DACA participants in the special immigrant juvenile program , which prohibits conferring immigration benefits on parents when recipients become lawful permanent residents .

I expect the Dignity Act of 2025 to be reintroduced in the next Congress. If it were enacted, however, it would make lawful status available to so many undocumented immigrants that their applications might destroy our already overwhelmed immigration system.

Its Dignity status program would be available to an unlimited number of undocumented immigrants who have been here continuously since Dec. 31, 2020, and the eligibility requirements for Dignity status would not establish that the recipients merit such relief.

Living in the United States that long does not establish that deportation would be a substantial hardship without additional hardship factors. And the rest of the requirements, such as paying $7,000 in restitution, would not establish that the recipients merit lawful status.

And who would process these applications? As of June 30, 2026, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services had a total pending caseload of 12.8 million cases.

On the other hand, the Dignity status benefit itself makes sense. It would just make it possible for these immigrants to live and work lawfully in the United States, without providing a path to permanent resident status or citizenship.

I recommend a modified version of Dignity status that requires good moral character, continuous employment or other productive activity, payment of taxes, and a favorable discretionary determination based on the applicant’s circumstances. It also should have a realistic numerical limitation.

The Immigration and Nationality Act included a registry provision when it was enacted in 1952 . It permits undocumented aliens to establish a record of admission as lawful permanent residents if they are not inadmissible or deportable under specified provisions in the law and they meet other eligibility requirements.

The current eligibility requirements require applicants to establish that they entered the United States prior to Jan. 1, 1972; have had continuous residence since then; have good moral character ; and that relief is merited as a matter of discretion.

The 1972 cut-off date was established by the Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986 , and it has not been updated since then. This means that it’s only available to undocumented immigrants who have been here at least 54 years.

Trump has suggested a deal with the Democrats to help immigrants who have been in the U.S. for 10 or 15 years and work in jobs such as landscaping or hotels. He might be willing to accept a registry update for a larger group of undocumented immigrants who have been here for 10 or 15 years.

Trump isn’t likely to give the Democrats the legalization programs they want, but they have no feasible alternative. They aren’t likely to pass any immigration reform bills into law without his support.

Nolan Rappaport was detailed to the House Judiciary Committee as an executive branch immigration law expert for three years. He subsequently served as an immigration counsel for the Subcommittee on Immigration, Border Security and Claims for four years. Prior to working on the Judiciary Committee, he wrote decisions for the Board of Immigration Appeals for 20 years.

articles.title: The wild world of modern penis enlargement
articles.summary: A new documentary explores the world of injectable penis filler, and why guys across the US are lining up for it.
articles.body: When Daniel Lombroso set about making “Manhood,” a documentary film tracing the meteoric rise of a new penile girth enhancement product in the US, he wasn’t sure if men would want to talk. There were teens aged 18 and 19 years old as well as men in their 70s, 80s and 90s. Most were straight, which surprised Lombroso. But “believe it or not, our success rate was pretty high,” he said in a video call from New York. Around half of the guys he met at a clinic in Dallas were willing to participate in his film — some comfortable showing their face but not their penis, others wanting the camera on their penis but not their face. At least one, he said, was more out-and-out proud: “I still get dick pics to this day.” The filmmaker and video journalist has spent the last three years investigating the popularity of Phallofill, a trademarked injectable procedure developed by Texan aesthetics practitioner Bill Moore. For weeks, Lombroso sat in Moore’s waiting room observing the stream of guys filter in to have their genitals enlarged with hyaluronic acid filler — the same substance at the center of this year’s Winter Olympics “penis-gate,” after a German newspaper alleged ski jumpers were using it to improve aerodynamics. The film shows us how this ancient male anxiety is being re-animated by the modern context of so-called “lunchtime” injectable filler. “I met a megachurch pastor getting his penis enlarged, a border patrol agent, a father of five, a brain cancer survivor, an OnlyFans star,” he said. “It felt like this incredible, unexpected portrait across America.” Men are now one of the fastest growing demographics for plastic surgery in the US, according to the American Academy of Facial Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery. Facelifts and facial fat grafts saw a bigger increase in male patients in 2025 compared with female patients. Some surgeries, such as Brazilian butt lifts and rhinoplasties, saw a rise in male patients even when the number of female patients dipped. “I think men are finally grappling with their own body dysmorphia, their own insecurities, the ways that they want to modify their appearance for the first time,” Lombroso said. Prescriptions for finasteride in the US, a popular hair regrowth medication, increased 200% between 2017 and 2024. Just last month, US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. decided to make non-US Food and Drug Administration approved peptides touted by online influencers for weight loss, muscle building and longevity available through compounding pharmacies across the country. “The film is not pro penis enlargement. It’s not anti penis enlargement. It’s using that as a canvas to explore this well of male insecurity that pervades so much of what we do, from the cultural level all the way to the political level,” Lombroso said. A central character of Lombroso’s film is Ruben, a Mexican American middle-aged father-of-five who works 12-hour-shifts to support his single-income household. Yet despite living on a hamster wheel of debt, Ruben was paying thousands per penis enlargement session with Moore. Over the course of the film, the financial pressure mounts, but his injections continue — even when Ruben’s partner Lana expresses complete disinterest and the family end up moving out of their home. It’s a baffling scenario made more legible when we learn about Ruben’s childhood sexual trauma, and observing what Lombroso calls the “passive noise” of his life: the manospheric podcasts we watch him absorb in the shower, while he drives and even when he’s eating dinner with his family. “These are podcasts that are telling you all the time that the way to be strong is to have a bigger penis, get a nicer car or who knows what, eat more elk meat,” he said. “Then here comes these practitioners on your feed that say, ‘I have a solution. I can cure your depression. I can help you get a promotion. You might become a CEO.’ ” Moore has built an empire promising men not only more inches, but access to some elusive charisma and power. “There definitely is something to the BDE, the Big Dick Energy,” Moore says in the film. “Everytime I call him, he’s busier, he’s in more locations,” said Lombroso. “And that’s only going to grow from there.” The documentary also shows urologists upskilling in Phallofill administration — something that concerned Lombroso. He thought many were pivoting away from “important work” with erectile dysfunction solutions to “basically Botox injections in your penis, because they see dollar signs.” As it turns out, the story of penis enlargement has many of the disparate threads that make up so much of our contemporary despair: financial insecurity, the loneliness of the digital world, loud polarizing media, the easy accessibility of cosmetic surgery. But at the heart of the documentary is empathy. “These men are a marketplace, and millions of dollars can be made off of them,” Lombroso said. “Usually the problem isn’t your penis. Usually the problem is a lot deeper.”

articles.title: Ecuadorian fishermen sue US over mysterious boat strike
articles.summary: Ecuadorian fishermen have filed a lawsuit against the US government over a mysterious attack against their boat involving small, explosive-laden rotor drones, their lawyer Jorge Chiriboga Dávalos announced Tuesday.
articles.body: Ecuadorian fishermen have filed a lawsuit against the US government over a mysterious attack against their boat involving small, explosive-laden rotor drones, their lawyer Jorge Chiriboga Dávalos announced Tuesday. The crew of La Negra Francisca Duarte II claims the US is to blame for the strike that sank their vessel on March 17 off the Galápagos Islands, within Ecuador’s exclusive economic zone. They say they were wrongfully targeted in the US military’s campaign against alleged drug-trafficking vessels. They are seeking compensation for their economic losses and physical injuries, as well as an injunction to end the United States’ deadly strikes against boats in the Pacific and Caribbean, according to American attorney Dan Kovalik, who filed the lawsuit along with Chiriboga on Monday in federal court in the western district of Pennsylvania. The lawsuit, which named the United States of America as the defendant, is demanding $5 million in damages. The US Defense Department has previously denied involvement in the attack. CNN has reached out to the US attorney general’s office for comment on the lawsuit. The US Southern Command told CNN it “does not comment on pending or ongoing litigation” as a matter of policy. Kovalik, who previously filed another lawsuit over a US strike that presumably killed a Colombian fisherman last year, told reporters Tuesday that they have proof the US was involved in the March 17 attack against La Negra Francisca’s fishermen, all of whom survived, some with serious injuries. He claimed the fishermen were subsequently detained on another ship by members of the US Navy and US Coast Guard and that at least one of the two drones involved in the attack was a US drone. Hours after the alleged strike, another fishing crew arrived at the site and took videos of the empty boat in flames, Chiriboga said. The lawsuit accuses the US of willfully attacking, kidnapping and torturing the fishermen. The US has acknowledged conducting dozens of lethal attacks on alleged drug-trafficking vessels in the Pacific and Caribbean, but La Negra Francisca Duarte II is not among the acknowledged incidents. In early March, the US began unspecified operations to target “designated terrorist organizations” in the South American country, according to the Pentagon. Kovalik said defense cooperation agreements between the US and Ecuador do not protect them from what he described as attempted murder. He insists that La Negra Francisca’s crew were not involved in drug trafficking. He noted that hours before this attack, the Ecuadorian Navy had boarded and inspected the boat and cleared the crew of any wrongdoing. “Even if that weren’t the case … the US has no right to be bombing boats in the Caribbean and the Pacific on the claim the people are narco-traffickers. If they believe someone is a narco-trafficker, they need to go get a warrant for their arrest,” Kovalik said. One of several unexplained attacks After La Negra Francisca’s fishermen were purportedly attacked and detained, they were transferred to a Salvadoran Coast Guard ship in the middle of the sea, the crew previously told CNN. From there, they were shipped away to El Salvador, where they stayed for several days before eventually being flown back to Manta, Ecuador, the coastal city from which their boat had departed. The lawsuit claims all the plaintiffs have lost their livelihood and are in “dire economic straits.” It also says they all suffer severe psychological trauma and that some are still dealing with physical pain, scarring and disability as a result of their injuries. The March 17 strike is one of three unexplained attacks against Ecuadorian fishing crews earlier this year. The vessel Don Maca experienced an almost identical attack on March 26, its crew members previously told CNN. Another Ecuadorian fishing boat called Fiorella disappeared during a fishing voyage on January 20, along with eight crew members, and is believed to have been attacked as well, according to Fernando Bastias, an attorney with Ecuador’s human rights committee. Attorney Chiriboga said the lawsuit is only being filed on behalf of La Negra Francisca’s crew. He added that the court will be asked to investigate if the CIA was involved in the attack, as the Washington Post reported.

The footage was recorded by another fishing crew passing by the area. The US Department of Defense has denied knowledge of or involvement in the incident.

articles.title: Actor Brian Cox backed a £100,000 appeal for a Scottish museum saved by women who stood before bulldozers; its 6,000 artefacts include objects linked to the 1692 Glencoe Massacre, with reopening planned for 2027
articles.summary: A riding boot linked to a military officer involved in one of Scotland's most infamous historical tragedies is among the objects preserved at a small
articles.body: A riding boot linked to a military officer involved in one of Scotland's most infamous historical tragedies is among the objects preserved at a small museum in the Highlands. Glencoe Folk Museum, which houses around 6,000 artefacts documenting the area's history, is undergoing a major redevelopment aimed at protecting its collection and making its exhibitions accessible to more visitors. According to the BBC, actor Brian Cox, known for his role in Succession, supported a £100,000 fundraising appeal for the institution in October 2025. A year later, the restoration is under way, but the museum remains closed, with its reopening now expected in 2027, according to its official museum website.Brian Cox supported the museum's £100,000 fundraising appealCox became involved in the campaign in October 2025, when Glencoe Folk Museum was seeking an additional £100,000 to complete its redevelopment. The appeal formed part of a much larger restoration project, for which approximately £2.8 million had already been secured from donors and funding organisations.The actor spoke about the importance of the museum to Scotland's cultural history, highlighting its collection and the stories associated with the Glencoe area. He also urged the public to contribute towards the work, which was initially expected to allow the museum to reopen in 2026.The funding shortfall had emerged as construction costs increased and delays affected the original plans. The museum had secured planning permission and listed building consent, but the rising expense of working on historic buildings meant some elements of the proposed redevelopment had to be reconsidered.Cox's appeal helped bring attention to an institution whose collection is closely connected to the history and identity of the local community.The museum preserves objects linked to the 1692 Glencoe MassacreAmong the most unusual items in the collection is a riding boot associated with Captain Robert Campbell, the officer who led the government troops involved in the Massacre of Glencoe. The boot was discovered in a boarded-up room at his former home in Glenlyon, Perthshire.According to The National Trust for Scotland, the object has a direct connection to the events of February 1692, when at least 38 members of the Macdonald clan were killed by soldiers who had been staying with them in Glencoe. The killings followed a period of political tension after members of the clan failed to meet a deadline to swear allegiance to the new monarchs, William III and Mary II.The massacre remains a significant episode in Scottish history, partly because the soldiers had been accommodated by the families they subsequently attacked. The incident became associated with a breach of Highland hospitality and left a lasting mark on the area's historical memory.The museum's plans include a dedicated exhibition exploring the killings. One of its historic cottages is being adapted to present the events through sound and visual displays, including lighting effects designed to recreate the atmosphere of an occupied Highland home.The wider collection also includes Jacobite objects and material from the two world wars, alongside possessions that document the everyday lives, work and traditions of people in the glen.Local women founded the museum after resisting demolitionGlencoe Folk Museum has its own unusual history. As reported by the BBC, it was established more than 50 years ago by local women who wanted to preserve two traditional cottages that were facing demolition. The founders reportedly stood in front of bulldozers to prevent the buildings from being destroyed. Their efforts eventually resulted in the creation of a museum dedicated to the history of the area.The institution has since become a repository for thousands of objects donated by local families. Its curator, Catriona Davidson, has previously described how people who visited the museum as children now return with their grandchildren. Some are able to recognise possessions that their own relatives contributed to the collection.£3 million raised as redevelopment work gets under wayThe restoration has taken longer than initially anticipated. Although the original target was to reopen in 2026, difficulties involving construction costs, inflation, procurement and the specialist work required for historic buildings pushed the timetable back. A significant development came in July 2026, when groundworks began at the museum site. The project had by then moved into its construction phase, following years of fundraising and preparation.By September 2026, Museums and Heritage Highland reported that approximately £3 million had been raised and that building work was well under way. The restoration has involved challenges within the original cottages, including structural issues uncovered after parts of the buildings were cleared.The museum's current reopening target is 2027, with the project team working towards Easter. It remains closed to visitors while the work continues.New gallery and improved facilities planned for visitorsThe redevelopment will introduce facilities that the museum has not previously been able to offer. These include a climate-controlled exhibition space, an accessible entrance, visitor toilets and an expanded gift shop. A separate community gallery is also planned inside a converted outbuilding. It will provide space for local groups, schools and other organisations to hold activities, exhibitions and meetings.The exhibition programme is being redesigned to cover different aspects of Glencoe's past, including the history of its cottages, the surrounding landscape, local families and the area's clan heritage. Environmental improvements are another part of the project. Better conditions inside the buildings will help protect the collection, while the redesigned spaces will allow the museum to consider borrowing objects from other institutions for future exhibitions.You use AI every day. articles.title: Israeli settler pogrom kills Palestinian woman, wounds 10 people
articles.summary: The Palestinian Health Ministry says Fadda Mohammed Fheidat, 72, was shot dead by Israeli settlers.
articles.body:
Israeli settlers have killed an elderly Palestinian woman and wounded 10 other people in a pogrom in the central occupied West Bank, the official Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.

The Palestinian Health Ministry named the woman killed as Fadda Mohammed Fheidat, 72.

The attack began early on Tuesday in the Duyuk al-Tahta neighbourhood on the outskirts of Jericho city, where settlers forcibly took over several properties earlier this month.

Witnesses told the news agency Reuters that a group of settlers began shooting outside Fheidat’s home, and Palestinian residents threw stones to defend themselves. More settlers arrived and fired at Palestinian homes, including Fheidat’s, the witnesses said.

Ahmed Aref, 62, Fheidat’s brother-in-law, said that a bullet hit her in the head as she stood in front of her house.

“I found her lying on the ground, with blood coming from her head,” he said.

The Israeli military did not comment on the woman’s death, but said it was dealing with “ongoing incidents” in which Israelis and Palestinians were wounded in an alleged car-ramming.

Fheidat’s son, Arafat, rushed to the scene after hearing she was hurt. His wife, Naama Fheidat, said he was in shock and accidentally hit a settler’s car parked in the driveway.

Witnesses said the settlers were not in the car, and that they then fired wildly, wounding several people, including Arafat, in the torso.

Arafat Fheidat said the Israeli military stopped the ambulance he was in as he was being taken to hospital in Ramallah and arrested him.

The military told Reuters a group of Palestinians in a car “accelerated their vehicle toward an Israeli vehicle and rammed it”, claiming that there were both Israeli and Palestinian casualties.

The settler attack comes about two weeks after settlers took over eight homes in Duyuk al-Tahta, the official Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.

The Binyamin Regional Council, which represents settlers in the area, said it had helped facilitate the move of families into eight homes purchased from Palestinians.

Jericho’s Palestinian governor, Hussein Hamayel, has said the settlers could not legally buy the land because it belongs to the state.

Israeli pogroms in the occupied West Bank have surged to what the United Nations has called an “unprecedented level”, following the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023 and the subsequent genocidal war on Gaza.

According to the UN, at least 1,143 Palestinians have been killed in the occupied West Bank since October 7, 2023, including 250 children.

The figure includes Palestinians killed by Israeli settlers living in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank.

The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) said 2026 is on track to be the most violent year for settler-related violence since it began monitoring the occupied West Bank a decade ago. In July alone, 11 people were killed in four incidents involving armed settlers alongside Israeli forces.

articles.title: J&K to mandate EWS quota in private school entry class
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: Jammu & Kashmir govt is set to reserve 25% of seats in the entry-level class in private unaided schools for children from economically weaker
articles.body: SRINAGAR: Jammu & Kashmir govt is set to reserve 25% of seats in the entry-level class in private unaided schools for children from economically weaker sections (EWS) and disadvantaged groups, in accordance with Section 12(1)(c) of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009.Education minister Shamim Firdous made this announcement during a meeting with representatives of private school associations, parents’ associations, and members of civil society in Srinagar Tuesday.“The rules governing the implementation of RTE Section 12(1)(c) are in the final stage and a notification will be issued shortly... The initiative is aimed at promoting inclusive education, ensuring equitable access to quality schooling and extending greater educational opportunities to children from underprivileged backgrounds,” she added.The govt will reimburse such schools for admissible expenditure incurred on implementing the scheme.The minister said that students must not be burdened with unnecessary additional or supplementary books, reiterating that the principles of NEP 2020 call for a balanced, flexible and child-centred approach to learning.“Where supplementary educational resources are considered necessary, schools may facilitate access through libraries, book banks, e-books and other digital learning resources rather than compelling parents to buy multiple additional books,” she added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Russian military plane crashes in Siberia killing all 19 on board
articles.summary: Russia's defence ministry says it preliminarily believes a technical malfunction was the cause of the crash in the Kemerovo region.
articles.body:
A Russian military transport plane has crashed in Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, the country's defence ministry said, according to state-run media.

The An-12 aircraft went down during a "scheduled flight" in an "uninhabited area" in the Kemerovo region, the ministry said in a statement.

The ministry added that it preliminarily believed a technical malfunction was the cause of Tuesday's crash. An investigation by Russia's aviation authorities is now under way.

Local Governor Ilya Seredyuk said an emergency response team "quickly extinguished a blaze" after the crash near the village of Yagunovo, and the area was sealed off by police.

Seredyuk, who visited the crash site, said "a helicopter and medical facilities have been put on standby".

The governor added that the "main task" now was to help investigators carry out their work.

He also posted a video showing firefighters combing through what looked like the crash debris, with a number of ambulances also seen standing nearby.

CCTV footage posted on social media appeared to show the moment the plane crashed, with a lighted object falling through the sky in the distance. An explosion then lit up the sky, but the crash was too far away to be seen.

The BBC and Reuters news agency verified the time and date of the footage, while Reuters also verified the location based on features of the scenery that matched satellite imagery of the area.

It was not immediately known whether the crashed aircraft had any cargo on board.

An-12 planes are widely used by the Russian military to transport weaponry and personnel, and also for search and rescue operations.

articles.title: Oxford protest against talk by academic who made Arday plagiarism claim
articles.summary: Nathan Cofnas accused late Cambridge professor Jason Arday of plagiarism.
articles.body:
Hundreds of people have gathered to protest against a talk at an Oxford University college by the academic who accused the late Professor Jason Arday of plagiarism.

Stand Up To Racism organised a demonstration against Nathan Cofnas's talk at Oriel College, organised by Oxford Reform UK, on Tuesday evening.

Protesters, some with face masks on, appeared to try to block the entrance gates to stop people getting into the college before the talk.

Dozens of protesters held signs saying "Nathan Cofnas not welcome" and "Remember Professor Jason Arday".

Chants of "Nathan Cofnas shut him down" could be heard.

It prompted a weeks-long plagiarism row that saw 41-year-old Arday face intense public scrutiny about his work and other achievements.

Although he denied the allegations made against him, Arday resigned his post as a Cambridge professor of sociology of education. He was found dead at his home in south London on 14 August.

Theo Biggs, 20, who is a student at nearby Oxford Brookes University, said: "Oxford University is a prestigious university, and what is talked about here is talked about around the world.

"Giving this sort of conversation a platform is legitimising it essentially."

A course administrator at the university, who did not want to be named, said: "I've seen a lot of students of colour are feeling unwelcome, uncomfortable, frightened by the fact that Oriel and the wider university has not shut this down."

Another student added: "I've worked really hard to get here. I pay a lot of money to be here, and then me being a minority is like the biggest sin in the world. It's not something I want, it's not something I'm standing for at all."

The talk's event page stated Cofnas "faced recent controversy after exposing the plagiarism of Jason Arday".

Cofnas has previously written that black people are less intelligent than other groups and would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment" under a meritocratic system.

He was suspended from Ghent University in Belgium in August before being reinstated after pressure by US ambassador Bill White.

On Thursday, protesters against the talk placed a Ku Klux Klan hood on a controversial statue of the 19th Century colonialist Cecil Rhodes at Oriel College.

In response to the protest, the college said it was "committed to upholding freedom of speech within the law and has a statutory duty to do so".

"We are also committed to promoting inclusion and maintaining an environment that is free from all forms of discrimination and harassment, including racial discrimination," it said.

It added that permitting the event "does not imply endorsement by the college of the views of its speakers".

articles.title: Vance’s midterm blame game hits snag as Trump’s own Israel ambassador disputes key claim
articles.summary: Mike Huckabee rejects JD Vance's claim that Israel cost Republicans the midterms, blaming voter apathy and low evangelical turnout for the GOP defeat.
articles.body: U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee is pushing back against Vice President JD Vance’s suggestion that America’s relationship with Israel contributed to Republicans’ crushing midterm election losses, offering a sharply different explanation from within the Trump administration. In an exclusive interview with The Press Service of Israel (TPS-IL) published Tuesday, Huckabee rejected the argument that Israel was responsible for the GOP’s electoral defeat, instead pointing to economic concerns, voter apathy and a failure to energize the Republican base. "Israel was not the reason the elections went wrong for Republicans last week," Huckabee told TPS-IL. TRUMP ADMITS IRAN WAR CONTRIBUTED TO GOP MIDTERM LOSSES, INSISTS IT WAS NECESSARY The remarks come nearly two weeks after Vance blamed Republican losses on the war with Iran and dissatisfaction with Washington’s relationship with Israel. In a Nov. 4 post on X, Vance argued, according to polling, that voters who supported the Trump-Vance ticket in 2024 had turned against Republicans over four key issues: ending the Iran war, addressing inflation and the cost of living, putting America first and changing the U.S. relationship with Israel. "The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote, arguing that the party needed to acknowledge the political consequences of the conflict. But Huckabee, a former Arkansas governor and longtime Evangelical leader, offered a competing assessment, arguing that Republicans had failed to give their own supporters sufficient motivation to vote. "To say that Israel was on the minds of most people is, I think, ludicrous," Huckabee told TPS-IL. Asked about Huckabee’s comments disputing the suggestion that the relationship with the State of Israel contributed to Republican losses in the midterms, a spokesperson for Vance told Fox News Digital: "The Vice President did not blame Jews for the Republican Party’s losses in the midterms. The Vice President has forcefully condemned antisemitism on countless occasions, and he will continue to do so." He acknowledged that the war may have influenced voters' perceptions, particularly as families struggled with higher fuel and food costs. "There’s no doubt that the war may have had some impact, not because it was the war itself, but there was such a media coverage that said that the war is what was creating the economic challenges," he said. REPUBLICANS SUFFER HISTORIC SENATE UPSET AS DEM FLIPS DEEP-RED STATE FOR FIRST TIME IN NEARLY A CENTURY "But it was the economic issues," Huckabee continued, adding that the war in Iran "may have contributed to prices, but it wasn't the only thing. There were a lot of factors involved." "If you look at the real numbers, the exit polls showed that only 17% of Evangelicals went and voted last week," Huckabee told TPS-IL. "There is no bloc of voters that is more critical to a Republican victory than Evangelical voters in the United States. They represent 80 million people. If they go vote in mass numbers, Republicans win, if they stay home, Republicans lose." The ambassador’s remarks referred to exit polling showing that white evangelical Christians accounted for 17% of voters in the 2026 midterms, compared with 23% in 2024. That figure reflects their share of the electorate, rather than the percentage of evangelicals who voted. "The real reason was that Republicans did not give even Republicans a good reason to go vote for them. They had the White House, they had the Senate, and they had the House. And if you ask the average American, what have they gotten done in the last two years? They could not provide for you very many, if anything, that the Congress had passed, accomplished, that they had expected them to get done." "So it's, it's unfortunate that Israel would factor in as a major reason for the vote in America," he added, "Because it just does not appear that that is as credible a reason as is that you had low turnout from the base of the Republican Party." TRUMP DRAWS RED LINE AGAINST NEWLY EMPOWERED DEMOCRATS, VOWING IMMEDIATE VETOES "The Democrats were excited. They went and voted in mass numbers, and they voted with enthusiasm. Enthusiasm wins elections; apathy does not." Beyond the dispute over the midterm elections, Huckabee warned that additional U.S. military action against Iran remains a possibility if Tehran refuses to abandon its nuclear ambitions, while expressing hope that a diplomatic solution could still be reached. "It's very possible that we will end up there, because if the Iranians do not understand what the president has made very clear, at least for the U.S. position, and that is they can't have a nuclear weapon," Huckabee told TPS-IL. "Is it possible to bring this to a resolution by diplomatic means or economic pressure? Hey, I would hope so. That would be wonderful. But if it can't be done, then the U.S, has made it clear, certainly the president, Secretary Rubio, have both said, just this week that the military option is every bit on the table." Huckabee said that Trump's position on Iran has remained consistent for decades, dating back to his years as a New York businessman in the early 1980s. He also pointed to the president's response to criticism that the war had contributed to Republican losses in the midterms. "He acknowledged, he said, it may have been a factor," Huckabee said. "And then he said, ‘But I would do it all over again.’" The ambassador defended that position, arguing that Trump's decision to confront Iran was driven by threats to American national security rather than political calculations. "It was because, for all these years, he's recognized the threat that they pose to America, not just to Israel," Huckabee said. PENCE DELIVERS SCATHING REBUKE OF VANCE'S IRAN WAR ASSESSMENT, BLAMES TRUMP POLICIES FOR GOP LOSSES He cited Americans killed by Iran and Iranian-backed groups over the past several decades, including U.S. casualties in Iraq and Afghanistan, and referred to the Americans killed and taken hostage during the Oct. 7 Hamas terror attacks. Huckabee praised Trump's willingness to accept potential political consequences, saying that even if the Iran issue had cost Republicans the election, the president would have made the same decision. "His job is not just to win in the election, [it] is to protect Americans," Huckabee said. "That's first and foremost, and I'm happy to have a president who knows that and who practices that." The ambassador also addressed Israel’s political future, saying Washington would work with whichever Israeli government emerges following the country’s elections, regardless of Trump’s close relationship with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. "The U.S. does not pick the government for Israel; the people do. However, it shakes up. We are committed to working with the government," he told TPS-IL. articles.title: US carries out self-defense strike on IRGC missile launch site on Qeshm Island
articles.summary: U.S. jets struck an IRGC missile site on Iran’s Qeshm Island Tuesday in self-defense, officials told Fox News.
articles.body: American fighter aircraft carried out a self-defense airstrike on an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) missile launch site on Qeshm Island, Iran, on Tuesday, two U.S. military officials confirmed to Fox News. "Earlier today, U.S. fighter aircraft used precision munitions to strike an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) missile launch site on Qeshm Island in self-defense. "The strike was in response to IRGC aggression targeting U.S. personnel and assets. U.S. Central Command remains highly vigilant and fully postured to protect Americans across the region," an official said in a statement. The strikes came hours after Tehran claimed it targeted a U.S. radar system at the Sheikh Isa base in Bahrain. IRAN’S DRONE HUNT ESCALATES AS TEHRAN TARGETS US SPY TECH TO EXPOSE BATTLEFIELD SECRETS In a statement, the IRGC claimed its operation was in response to violations of Iran's airspace by U.S. drones and said the action was taken to counter "hostile U.S. movements in the region," according to the semi-official, state-sponsored Mehr News Agency. CENTCOM said later the Iranian attack drones were all intercepted. "Multiple Iranian one-way attack drones launched by the IRGC today towards Bahrain were intercepted without any damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel," the command said in a post shared on X. Qatar also went on to condemn Iran's ongoing attacks on Bahrain on Tuesday, calling them a violation of Bahraini sovereignty. articles.title: Lane Kiffin admits to waking up every hour with recurring nightmare of LSU's loss to Texas
articles.summary: Lane Kiffin says he wakes up every hour haunted by nightmares of the final play as LSU's 22-21 loss to Texas ended the Tigers' playoff hopes.
articles.body: LSU head coach Lane Kiffin can't stop thinking about his team's gut-wrenching loss to Texas. He can't even escape the torture of reliving the dramatic finish while he's sleeping. With the Longhorns handing LSU its fourth loss of the season, the Tigers' College Football Playoff dreams officially died on Saturday night. To make matters even worse, the loss came inside Tiger Stadium in Baton Rouge in what was LSU's final home game of the season. For many LSU fans, the terrible taste in their mouths will linger until the Tigers earn an impressive win in 2027. That may seem dramatic, but that is SEC football in southeastern Louisiana. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Kiffin and the rest of his coaching staff need to be the first to forget about the 22-21 loss to Texas, as deflating as it was, given that the Tigers still have to take on Tennessee and Arkansas on the road to end the season. Unfortunately for Kiffin, his brain isn't allowing it. "I'll wake up literally every hour the last two nights, and I have this nightmare of the last play of the game, but I think it's a nightmare that we didn't cover somebody to lose the game, and that we lost to Texas," Kiffin told the media on Monday, nearly 48 hours after the game. articles.title: Russian military transport plane crashes in Siberia, killing 19, according to Defense Ministry
articles.summary: MOSCOW — A Russian military transport plane crashed in western Siberia on Tuesday, killing all 19 people on board, the Defense Ministry said.
articles.body: MOSCOW — A Russian military transport plane crashed in western Siberia on Tuesday, killing all 19 people on board, the Defense Ministry said. Preliminary findings pointed to equipment failure. The An-12 aircraft went down in an unpopulated area near the village of Yagunovo, in the Kemerovo region, about 3,000 kilometers (about 1,860 miles) east of Moscow. The ministry said all 19 people on board, including the crew, were killed. Air force experts were investigating the cause of the crash. The An-12 typically has a crew of six. The An-12 is a Soviet-built four-engine turboprop transport plane that has been in service since the late 1950s. Over 1,000 were built and some still remain in operation in Russia and other nations.
