articles.title: Israel’s parliament elects new Knesset speaker, weakening Netanyahu’s grip on power
articles.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s grip on power suffered a critical blow on Tuesday as parliament voted to elect a new speaker, giving the opposition greater control over the legislative agenda.
articles.body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s grip on power suffered a critical blow on Tuesday as parliament voted to elect a new speaker, giving the opposition greater control over the legislative agenda. The Knesset elected Matan Kahana of Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party as its 26th speaker, replacing Amir Ohana, from Netanyahu’s Likud party. Kahana received the support of 66 lawmakers, according to the Knesset spokesperson. Lawmakers voted separately on the candidates, rather than in a head-to-head ballot. Likud’s candidate, coalition whip Ofir Katz, received the support of 52 lawmakers in a separate vote. The vote marks the first significant move by the Eisenkot-led bloc to set a new direction for the legislature since Netanyahu lost his Knesset majority in the October 27 elections. The prime minister and his coalition of right-wing and ultra-Orthodox parties won only 53 seats in the 120-seat parliament. The opposition holds 67 seats, including 48 across four Jewish parties and a record 19 for two Arab parties: the Joint List and Raam. Eisenkot, who was tasked by President Isaac Herzog earlier this month with forming the next government, has up to four and a half more weeks to replace Netanyahu, but his path to power remains difficult. However, his bloc now controls the Knesset plenum, key positions, and legislative agenda, and plans to use them to scrutinize and constrain Netanyahu’s caretaker government, which remains in office until it is replaced. Eisenkot said Tuesday that Kahana’s appointment is a “proper democratic move which reflects the absolute majority who voted for change.” Eisenkot’s bloc has already appointed interim chairs for key Knesset committees, including finance and defense, expanding oversight and control over the budget and strategic affairs. Avigdor Liberman, the leader of the opposition Yisrael Beitenu party now chairing the Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, has already said he would summon all the security chiefs for briefings. One of the opposition’s top legislative priorities is to undo judicial overhauls from Netanyahu’s outgoing coalition that sparked unprecedented nationwide protests in 2023. Critics of the overhaul said it weakened Israel’s democratic institutions and judicial oversight of the government. Special committees have already been established to repeal a bill that changed how judges were selected and legislation that limits and weakens the attorney general. A separate committee was formed to undo a media regulation overhaul which expanded government control over the communications and news sector. Eisenkot’s bloc has also pledged to advance the establishment of a state commission of inquiry into the failures that led to the Hamas-led attack on October 7, 2023, which Netanyahu has refused to investigate. Netanyahu and his allies tried to block Kahana’s election and to delegitimize it as dependent on the support of the Arab parties, even though they themselves have repeatedly sought support from Arab lawmakers in parliament. During the vote, members of Netanyahu’s bloc shouted “shame” at each Arab lawmaker who voted in support of Kahana. Likud condemned the outcome after the vote, calling it “a low point in the history of the Knesset” and saying Kahana had been elected with the votes of what it called “terror supporters.” Obstacles to replacing Netanyahu While Eisenkot and his allies have seized control of the Knesset, his plan to replace Netanyahu still faces significant obstacles. Eisenkot wanted to form what he calls a “national emergency government,” a minority government made of the four Jewish opposition parties, which together hold 48 seats. The Arab parties would stay out of the coalition but would guarantee a majority in the Knesset to keep the government from collapsing in exchange for various concessions. But other leaders in Eisenkot’s bloc are pushing in different directions. Liberman has vetoed any government that relies on the Arab parties’ support and is pushing for talks with the two ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism (UTJ), which have been traditionally allied with Netanyahu. UTJ, the Ashkenazi ultra-Orthodox party, declined to recommend Netanyahu for the premiership in the post-election consultations and has opened the door to informal talks with Eisenkot’s bloc. But it did not support Kahana in the vote for speaker of the Knesset, instead supporting Likud’s candidate. The second ultra-Orthodox party, Shas, remains loyal to Netanyahu, leaving Liberman’s strategy uncertain. Another obstacle is former prime minister Naftali Bennett, who reportedly favors talks on a unity government with Netanyahu’s Likud party over an alliance with the Arab or ultra-Orthodox parties. However, Netanyahu has conditioned any talks on him remaining prime minister, which Eisenkot has rejected, raising doubts Bennett’s vision can succeed.

articles.title: UK hands NATO-assigned US soldier accused of Russia spying to US military
articles.summary: UK authorities have passed the investigation to the US ‘in line with existing international protocols’.
articles.body:
A senior United States soldier assigned to NATO who was arrested in Britain last week on suspicion of spying for Russia has been transferred to US military custody, United Kingdom police have said.

The Head of Counter Terrorism Police (CTP), Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, said on Tuesday that authorities in London have passed the investigation to US partners “in line with existing international protocols”.

The 41-year-old man was arrested by British police on November 10 near Gloucester on suspicion of offences under Section 1 and Section 3 of the UK National Security Act 2023.

Section 1 relates to obtaining or disclosing protected information, while Section 3 relates to assisting a foreign intelligence service.

“These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place,” Taylor said.

He added, “We will continue to support our US colleagues as they take the matter forwards.”

US FBI Director Kash Patel said the army officer is in US custody as a “result of an espionage investigation” between the FBI’s Philadelphia field office and Legat London in addition to partners at “UK Counter Terrorism Policing, MI5, UK Defence Counter Intelligence, and the US Army Counterintelligence Command.”

Brigadier General Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command (ACIC), said the case illustrated the “remarkable partnership” between ACIC, US Army prosecutors, the FBI, the US Department of Justice, and the UK.

Stinchon added that this example sends a “stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath”.

The case is believed to be the first time a US soldier was found to be under suspicion of spying for a foreign government while in the UK.

articles.title: Board of Peace delivers bleak report on Gaza, warning of ceasefire collapse without immediate action
articles.summary: NEW YORK — The body overseeing the U.S.-brokered ceasefire in Gaza delivered another bleak report Tuesday on its progress to the United Nations Security Council, warning diplomats of a collapse of the fragile agreement if steps are not taken for full implementation.
articles.body: NEW YORK — The body overseeing the U.S.-brokered ceasefire in Gaza delivered another bleak report Tuesday on its progress to the United Nations Security Council, warning diplomats of a collapse of the fragile agreement if steps are not taken for full implementation. The Board of Peace report calls on both Israel and Hamas to uphold the commitments made last year under the agreement and urges the U.N.’s most powerful body to lend its support to the execution. “The distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground nonetheless remains the principal risk to the process,” says the report, a copy of which was obtained by The Associated Press. It is the latest admonishment from the board in recent weeks as deadly Israeli strikes and the continued blocking of humanitarian aid to Gaza have caused widespread devastation to the civilian population, which the board says is set to face “another winter in tents and rubble.” “Restrictions imposed by Israel on the entry of supplies and equipment, compounded by funding shortfalls, continued to impede preparedness and response efforts,” the report said, calling for immediate “scaled-up entry of shelter and winterization materials” and approvals for pumps, generators and heavy machinery. The board’s first report was delivered in May by its director-general Nickolay Mladenov, who formerly served as a U.N. Mideast envoy. At the time, Mladenov had acknowledged to the Security Council that the truce brokered by President Donald Trump had stalled since taking effect in October of last year, saying the deadlock over disarming Hamas had paralyzed progress. The report released this week echoes those same issues six months later, pointing out how continued Israeli strikes in Gaza and Hamas military activity have stalled efforts for both sides to adhere to the road map. “A ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely,” the report said. “Should it collapse, there would be no road map to return to, no administration to deploy and no enabling environment to rebuild.” Apart from continued fighting, the report laments that the technocratic civil administration the board created to run Gaza on an interim basis has still not been allowed by Israel to take up its job in the territory. “The absence of decisions by the government of Israel on the necessary conditions and arrangements for the training, deployment and return of civilian police to Gaza continues to impede full implementation of the Comprehensive Plan,” the report said. “The Board of Peace calls on the government of Israel to take these decisions without delay.” The lack of approvals has, in turn, delayed deployment of an international stabilization force, which is key to Israel’s withdrawal of troops from Gaza, the disarmament of Hamas and the start of reconstruction. To get things moving, the board appealed to the Security Council to put its full weight behind the agreement it endorsed last year and urge the parties to stop delays. “Neither party may treat the other’s delay as license for its own inaction, and together these obligations are the only route to Israeli withdrawal and reconstruction at scale,” the report said. It added that the end result “must lead to the credible pathway to Palestinian self-determination and statehood … and no unilateral step should be allowed to foreclose it.”

articles.title: Ukraine talks yielding progress: Kushner
articles.summary: Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law, said he and fellow U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff are “making progress” toward bringing an end to war in Ukraine — though “important challenges” remain. “A final agreement will require difficult decisions. But we are making progress, in close coordination with Russia, Ukraine, and Europe, toward an outcome that can…
articles.body:
Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law, said he and fellow U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff are “making progress” toward bringing an end to war in Ukraine — though “important challenges” remain.

“A final agreement will require difficult decisions. But we are making progress, in close coordination with Russia, Ukraine, and Europe, toward an outcome that can end this war, strengthen European security, and create the foundations for lasting peace,” Kushner wrote in a post to social platform X Monday.

Kushner said he and Witkoff spoke with Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov Monday morning to discuss the peace negotiations, a statement which came after he shared last week that Russian leadership agreed to bring European partners into the talks. He added there was also a “productive call” this week between Ukrainian and European officials.

“We discussed how to facilitate direct engagement between Europe and Russia, which has been largely absent over the past four years,” he said. “It is important that both sides hear each other’s concerns and proposals directly as we work toward a more stable and secure future for Europe.”

Last week, Kushner announced Russia had agreed to European participation in the negotiations to end the war after a visit to Moscow. However, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov signaled officials may not have committed to bringing more parties into the discussion.

“Once we understand their genuine intention and readiness to contribute to the peace process, then it will be possible to make a decision on holding dialogue on a Ukrainian settlement in an expanded format,” Peskov said Friday.

“Our objective is to build on Europe’s existing institutions and agreements, strengthening security commitments, communication, transparency, and mechanisms for de-escalation so that the peace we achieve can endure,” Kushner said in his Monday post.

Moscow and Kyiv held their first U.S.-mediated talks in nine months last week in Abu Dhabi, during which they agreed to a “large-scale” exchange of prisoners of war, as Russia’s war against Ukraine approaches the five-year mark.

“Any final peace agreement will need to be agreed to by both Russia and Ukraine,” Kushner said in his post.
